overview:
In Jainism, cosmological maps are visual and textual representations of the structure of the loka, the finite world-space within the infinite cosmos. They do not depict a created universe with a beginning or end, but an eternal, cyclic reality whose spatial and temporal patterns are described with remarkable mathematical precision. These maps serve as pedagogical tools, ritual objects, and meditative aids, helping laypeople and monks alike to understand where liberation (mokṣa) is possible and how the soul’s journey unfolds within the three realms of existence.

At the broadest level, Jain cosmology divides the loka into three regions: the upper world (ūrdhva-loka), the middle world (madhya-loka), and the lower world (adho-loka). A key visual schema is the loka-puruṣa, the "cosmic person," in which the entire structured universe is projected onto a human-shaped figure. In this mapping, the realm of liberated souls (siddha-śilā) is located at the crown or forehead, the many heavens occupy the torso, the middle world is situated around the waist or belly, and the seven hells extend through the lower body. This anthropomorphic diagram emphasizes symmetry and hierarchy: spiritual elevation is literally mapped upward, while bondage and suffering are mapped downward. The loka-puruṣa diagram is grounded in descriptive passages found in cosmological compendia such as the Saṃgrahaṇī texts and later commentaries, which specify the dimensions and relative positions of these regions.

Within the middle world, Jain cosmological maps focus especially on the Aḍhāī-dvīpa (Two-and-a-Half Continents) configuration. At the center lies Jambūdvīpa (Jambudvīpa), the "Rose-Apple Continent," which includes the region of Bhāratakṣetra (Bharata), understood as the human realm corresponding to historical India, and Mahāvideha, a region where Tīrthaṅkaras are perpetually present. Surrounding Jambūdvīpa are concentric rings of oceans and continents: first the Lavaṇa-samudra (Salt Ocean), then Dhātakīkhaṇḍa-dvīpa, followed by the Kālodaḍhi (Black Water Ocean), and the inner half of Puṣkaradvīpa. Beyond the serrated mountain ring at the outer edge of Puṣkaradvīpa, humans cannot travel. Cloth paintings, lithographs, and manuscript diagrams depict these rings with labeled landmasses, rivers, mountain ranges (including Mount Meru at the center), and populated regions, closely following textual descriptions in works like the Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti and Saṃgrahaṇī-ratna.

These maps are not merely geographic; they are ethical and soteriological. The middle world is the only realm in which human birth occurs and where the path to liberation can be actively pursued. The presence of Tīrthaṅkaras in specific regions, the classification of lands into areas where right faith (samyag-darśana) is possible or impossible, and the depiction of temples with Jina images at the corners of cosmological maps all underscore that spiritual opportunity is spatially situated. In many painted maps, the vertical axis is marked by enshrined Jinas, visually linking the cartographic representation of continents and oceans to the lineage of enlightened teachers.

Jain cosmological maps also extend downward and upward beyond the Aḍhāī-dvīpa. Diagrams of the seven hells (adho-loka) show stacked levels of suffering, each with its own name and characteristics, while maps of the heavens (ūrdhva-loka) depict multiple tiers of celestial abodes, culminating in the siddha-śilā where liberated souls reside in a state beyond movement and rebirth. Texts such as the Tiloya-paṇṇatti and the cosmology sections of the Tattvārtha-sūtra provide numerical measures for these realms, including vast distances and lifespans, which are sometimes inscribed directly onto visual maps. The combination of precise numbers, named regions, and symbolic imagery reflects a distinctive Jain concern with both exactness and moral meaning.

Historically, cosmological maps appear in illustrated manuscripts, independent cloth paintings (paṭas), and later printed lithographs. They are found across Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions, with variations in artistic style, script, and regional emphasis, but a shared underlying structure derived from canonical and post-canonical cosmological treatises. Some maps emphasize the human world (manuṣya-loka) and Aḍhāī-dvīpa; others foreground the loka-puruṣa or the sequence of hells and heavens. Scholars have noted that while the core spatial schema is stable, details such as the depiction of specific mountain ranges, the iconography of aquatic creatures in the oceans, or the placement of certain regions can differ between manuscripts and paintings, reflecting local artistic conventions and interpretive choices.

Modern study of Jain cosmological maps draws on primary texts (Tier A), traditional commentaries (Tier B), and art-historical and Indological scholarship (Tier C). There is broad agreement on the basic tripartite division of the loka, the centrality of Jambūdvīpa and Aḍhāī-dvīpa, and the anthropomorphic loka-puruṣa schema. However, there are areas of uncertainty and debate, including the exact historical evolution of specific map types, the degree to which certain numerical values should be read literally or symbolically, and the relationship between regional map traditions and pan-Jain cosmological doctrine. Translations of Prakrit and Sanskrit cosmological passages can vary, especially for technical terms and large numerical units, so careful comparison of editions and commentaries is important when using these maps for academic or religious study.

In practice, cosmological maps continue to be used in Jain communities as objects of teaching and contemplation. They are displayed in temples, museums, and homes, and are sometimes engaged in ritual contexts, though they are not themselves objects of worship in the same sense as Jina images. For students of Jainism, these maps offer a vivid entry point into the tradition’s sophisticated cosmology, but they must be read alongside the primary texts that define their structure and meaning. When questions arise about how to apply cosmological teachings to modern ethical or spiritual decisions, consultation with qualified teachers from living lineages is recommended, since visual maps alone cannot provide binding guidance on practice.

primary_sources.title: Saṃgrahaṇī-ratna (also known as Trailokya-dīpikā in some recensions)
primary_sources.author: Dharmasāgara (Śvetāmbara tradition, attributed)
primary_sources.original_text: लोको नाम त्रिभेदोऽयं ऊर्ध्वमधोमध्यभेदतः । तत्र मध्यो मनुष्याणां मोक्षमार्गस्य च स्थितिः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration: loko nāma tribhedo’yaṃ ūrdhvam adho madhya-bhedataḥ | tatra madhyo manuṣyāṇāṃ mokṣa-mārgasya ca sthitiḥ ||
primary_sources.translation: The world-space (loka) is said to be threefold, divided into upper, lower, and middle. In that, the middle is the abode of humans and the place where the path to liberation is found.
primary_sources.notes: This verse summarizes the tripartite division of the loka and explicitly links the middle world (madhya-loka) to human existence and the possibility of liberation. Saṃgrahaṇī-ratna is a key cosmological compendium in the Śvetāmbara tradition, often accompanied by diagrams of the loka-puruṣa and maps of Aḍhāī-dvīpa. Different manuscripts may vary slightly in wording; the cited form reflects a commonly printed edition.

primary_sources.title: Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the canonical Śvetāmbara corpus (Āgama literature)
primary_sources.original_text: जम्बूद्वीपो नाम द्वीपः, तत्र मेरुर्नाम पर्वतो मध्ये स्थितः । तं पर्वतं परिक्रम्य लवणसमुद्रो नाम समुद्रः, तस्य परे धातकीखण्डद्वीपो नाम द्वीपः ।
primary_sources.transliteration: jambūdvīpo nāma dvīpaḥ, tatra merur nāma parvato madhye sthitaḥ | taṃ parvataṃ parikramya lavaṇa-samudro nāma samudraḥ, tasya pare dhātakī-khaṇḍa-dvīpo nāma dvīpaḥ |
primary_sources.translation: There is a continent called Jambūdvīpa, and in its center stands a mountain named Meru. Encircling that mountain is an ocean called Lavaṇa-samudra (Salt Ocean), and beyond it lies a continent called Dhātakī-khaṇḍa-dvīpa.
primary_sources.notes: This passage describes the central continent Jambūdvīpa, Mount Meru, and the first surrounding ocean and continent. It provides the textual basis for the concentric-ring structure seen in cosmological maps of Aḍhāī-dvīpa. The Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti-sūtra is part of the Śvetāmbara canonical cosmological texts; exact wording can differ between editions and Prakrit/Sanskrit reconstructions.

primary_sources.title: Tiloya-paṇṇatti (Triloka-prajñapti)
primary_sources.author: Yativṛṣabha (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text: एगल्लोको अणंतो, तस्स लोयकासे तु विण्णो, उव्वो अद्धो मज्झो, तिहि भेदो लोयओ ।
primary_sources.transliteration: egalloko aṇanto, tassa loyakāse tu viṇṇo, uvvo addho majjho, tihi bhedo loyao |
primary_sources.translation: The single cosmos is infinite, but within it the world-space (loka-ākāśa) is distinguished; it is divided into three: upper, lower, and middle world.
primary_sources.notes: Composed in Jaina Śaurasenī Prakrit, Tiloya-paṇṇatti is a major Digambara cosmological treatise. This verse parallels Śvetāmbara descriptions of the threefold loka and underlies Digambara visual traditions of the loka-puruṣa and related maps. Transliterations and translations vary slightly among modern editors; the version here follows a commonly cited reading.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (also called Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.transliteration: ūrdhvam adho madhyeṣu triṣu lokeṣu jīvāḥ |
primary_sources.translation: Living beings exist in the three worlds: upper, lower, and middle.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha-sūtra is a foundational philosophical text accepted by both Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions. This concise sūtra affirms the distribution of living beings across the three realms, a doctrinal basis for cosmological mapping. Commentaries elaborate the specific locations and types of beings, which are then depicted in visual cosmological diagrams.

primary_sources.title: Saṃgrahaṇī texts on Aḍhāī-dvīpa (representative prose passage)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous compilers; later commentators such as Devendra and others
primary_sources.original_text: अधाइद्वीपे जम्बूद्वीपधातकीखण्डद्वीपपुष्करद्वीपानां मध्ये मनुष्यलोकः प्रतिष्ठितः, तत्रैव जिनानां तीर्थानां च प्रादुर्भावः ।
primary_sources.transliteration: adhāi-dvīpe jambūdvīpa-dhātakī-khaṇḍa-dvīpa-puṣkara-dvīpānāṃ madhye manuṣya-lokaḥ pratiṣṭhitaḥ, tatraiva jinānāṃ tīrthānāṃ ca prādurbhāvaḥ |
primary_sources.translation: In the Two-and-a-Half Continents (Aḍhāī-dvīpa), comprising Jambūdvīpa, Dhātakī-khaṇḍa-dvīpa, and Puṣkara-dvīpa, the human world is established; there, indeed, the manifestations of the Jinas and their sacred fords (tīrthas) occur.
primary_sources.notes: This type of prose description, found in Saṃgrahaṇī manuscripts and related cosmological handbooks, explains that the human world and the appearance of Jinas are confined to the Aḍhāī-dvīpa structure. Such passages are often written around or within cosmological maps in manuscripts and paintings, labeling continents, oceans, and sacred sites. Exact wording differs by manuscript; the sentence here is a synthesized representation based on standard descriptions.

misconceptions.myth: Jain cosmological maps are purely symbolic or mythological and have no internal logic or structure.
misconceptions.reality: Jain cosmological maps follow detailed, internally consistent descriptions found in primary texts such as Saṃgrahaṇī-ratna, Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti, Tiloya-paṇ्णatti, and Tattvārtha-sūtra. They specify dimensions, relative positions, and classifications of beings with mathematical precision. While modern readers may debate whether certain numerical values are literal or symbolic, the maps themselves are not arbitrary illustrations but carefully constructed diagrams grounded in a coherent cosmological system.

misconceptions.myth: The loka-puruṣa (cosmic person) diagram implies that Jainism teaches a human-shaped creator deity who fashions the universe.
misconceptions.reality: The loka-puruṣa is an anthropomorphic diagram of the structured world-space, not a depiction of a creator god. Jain doctrine explicitly denies a creator deity and affirms an eternal, beginningless cosmos. The human-shaped outline is a visual device used to organize and relate the upper, middle, and lower worlds, emphasizing symmetry and hierarchy, rather than a theological claim about divine embodiment.

misconceptions.myth: Only one standardized Jain cosmological map exists, and all sects and regions use identical diagrams.
misconceptions.reality: While the underlying cosmological structure—three worlds, Aḍhāī-dvīpa, Jambūdvīpa, Mount Meru, and so on—is shared across Jain traditions, there are multiple map types and regional styles. Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities, as well as different regions of India, have produced varied cloth paintings, manuscript diagrams, and printed maps. Artistic conventions, scripts, and certain details differ, even though they are all anchored in the same core textual cosmology.

misconceptions.myth: Cosmological maps themselves are objects of worship equivalent to Jina images.
misconceptions.reality: Cosmological maps are primarily pedagogical and contemplative tools. They may be displayed in temples and homes and treated respectfully, but they are not generally the central focus of worship in the way that Jina mūrtis are. Their function is to illustrate the structure of the universe and the location of the path to liberation, not to serve as icons of divine presence.

misconceptions.myth: The presence of Bhāratakṣetra (Bharata) on cosmological maps means that Jain texts describe modern political India and its borders.
misconceptions.reality: Bhāratakṣetra in Jain cosmology is a religious-geographical region within Jambūdvīpa, defined by cosmological and ethical criteria, not by modern political boundaries. Although it is often associated with the broader Indian subcontinent, its extent and characteristics are determined by scriptural descriptions of karmic conditions, the presence of Tīrthaṅkaras, and cycles of spiritual decline and renewal, rather than contemporary national borders.
